A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FOSP and retain identifiable methods and experiments. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Safety-Gymnasium experiments, component ablations and Franka robot transfer results, including Tables 1–2 and appendix learning curves.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation and robot results and adds dataset ablations, transfer experiments, visual-shift tests and Race2 evaluations.

M1.justification: Online action selection changes from reward Q alone in v1 Equation 9 to normalized reward Q minus cost Q in v2 Equations 21–22. The reported critic objectives also change from likelihood losses to squared-error expressions. These affect central selection and optimization procedures, beyond renaming policy expansion.

E1.justification: The five original simulation tasks and three robot transfers remain. v2 adds PointGoal1-to-PointGoal2 transfer, SafetyFadingEasy1/Hard1 with disappearing visual information, SafetyPointBuildingGoal1 with substantially different visual inputs, and Race2 navigation. These introduce distinct transfer conditions and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds model-based Recovery RL to the shared offline-to-online comparisons and CPO and PPO-Lagrangian to online comparisons. Appendix E also adds a qualitative SafeDreamer comparison on the retained robot transfer tasks. SafeDreamer with online planning was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols vary safe/unsafe/random data proportions, dataset sizes of 300/600/900 trajectories, transfer environments and direct-online versus pretrained initialization. CPO and PPO-Lagrangian receive 10M training steps. The stated SafeDreamer planning budget changes from 1.5M steps in v1 Table 1 to 0.5M in v2 Table 2 despite unchanged scores; this establishes revised reporting, not necessarily rerunning.

E4.justification: The four component ablations are retained. v2 substantially expands analysis through dataset-composition and size sensitivity, direct-online versus fine-tuning controls, transfer adaptation curves, robot trajectory cases and a major visual-shift failure test (Section 5.3 and Appendix H).

E5.justification: The shared comparison and component-ablation captions change from three seeds to five, with v2 explicitly describing independent runs. This revises reported run counts without establishing which experiments were rerun. Both versions display variability bands without clearly defining them; no significance-testing framework is added.

E6.justification: Shared main-table scores for FOSP, DreamerV3 and SafeDreamer are retained. Reported robot post-fine-tuning success/violation percentages change from 50/30 to 65/20, 35/40 to 60/30, and 50/30 to 50/20 across the three tasks. Numerous new comparator, sensitivity and transfer results are added, including failure under substantial visual changes.

T1.justification: The three existing propositions and optimal-policy derivation are retained and reorganized. Bounded mathematical revisions include augmented-Lagrangian coefficients and finite-horizon expressions. The REF changes from reaching a feasible state in v1 to avoiding violations in v2 Section 4.2, although its formulations in Section 3 and Appendix B remain inconsistent.

C1.justification: The novelty claim shifts from the first model-based safe offline-to-online approach to the first offline-to-online approach addressing safe generalization. The central safety, performance and few-shot adaptation claims already appear in v1. The contribution list replaces the promised code/dataset release with an explicit few-trial adaptation contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains how dataset imbalance biases world-model cost predictions and produces aggressive or conservative policies. It adds substantive qualifications concerning expected-cost safety versus tail risk, failure under major visual changes, and difficulties with real-time control and dynamic obstacles. These extend v1's existing dataset-dependence, occlusion and tuning limitations.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the REF learning rate, 500,000-step robot pretraining, trajectory-based online updates and implementation details for added baselines. Hardware and most existing hyperparameters remain unchanged. The code/dataset release promise disappears, while a video-page link is added; the PDFs do not establish actual code availability.

R1.justification: The related-work foundation remains largely intact. v2 adds references including Recovery RL, SAC, PPO, PID-Lagrangian methods and additional reachability work, and reframes the relationship to policy expansion around safety. Novelty positioning shifts toward safe generalization without a wholesale replacement of the research context.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around safe generalization. The safety and policy-expansion method subsections exchange order, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and existing proofs and pseudocode receive separate appendix subsections. Explanations and limitations are extensively revised beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the framework diagram and separates the safety schematic, splits the main comparison table, and relocates and expands existing learning-curve displays. It adds dataset-ablation charts, transfer plots and robot trajectory panels. Figure 14 redisplays existing online results with fewer baselines for readability rather than adding evidence.

improvement.justification: v1's generalization evidence was limited to three robot transfers without a corresponding baseline comparison. v2 adds controlled simulation transfers, a qualitative robot baseline, dataset sensitivity and pretraining controls, and an informative visual-transfer failure. These substantially strengthen validation and clarify applicability. Ambiguous signs in the revised critic losses and inconsistent REF definitions limit technical clarity, but the added controls and explicit failure analysis provide a substantial net quality gain.
